setupSteps: High-to-low (pulleys above the head, hands finish low in front of the hips or navel). Most sources say it emphasises the lower chest; some sources (Fitnessvolt, Boostcamp) say the effect depends on the exact pulley angle and can reach the middle or even the upper chest. Treat this as an option, not a rule.

Mid (pulleys at about shoulder height, or just above, hands finish in front of the chest). ACE and Muscle & Strength both describe pulleys about at or slightly above shoulder height for the standing fly. A boxrox article ties the mid setting to the sternal (middle) chest, citing a 1995 study that was not checked.

Low-to-high (pulleys as low as possible, hands finish in front of the upper chest or chin). Most sources describe this as upper-chest and front-shoulder work; Muscle & Strength says to set both pulleys as low as possible.

FitPlate start: mid, with both pulleys at the same height. Add high-to-low and low-to-high later for variety once the arc is smooth. Always set both pulleys to the same height and the same load; check the height-adjust pins or levers are fully seated.

Single D-handles (or stirrup handles) on both cables are the standard. Clip each handle to its pulley snap hook and check the gate is closed and the handle is not cracked. Some gyms also have a single wide bar; avoid it for flies.
Check the cable: look for fraying, kinks or a stuck pulley; tell staff if the cable looks damaged (inspection steps are common practice; no formal standard was found).
Wrist straps are not needed. Hold the handle with a firm, not white-knuckle grip, thumb around the handle.

Pick a light load first. Put the pin in the lowest weight plate, or the second plate, on both stacks (the same on both sides). A beginner load is one you can control for 10–12 reps with 3–4 reps left (est.; see section 7).
Push the pin all the way in so it cannot fall out; re-check before you take the handles.
If the two stacks use different units or the pins are unmarked, ask staff which plate is which; do not guess.
Stand in the middle of the frame, halfway between the two stacks, one step in front of the pulley line (about 30–60 cm forward, est.) so the cables pull from slightly behind you.

Staggered (split) stance: one foot a stride in front of the other, front knee slightly bent, back leg supporting; weight mainly on the front foot. Gymnation says the staggered stance keeps tension on the chest while limiting shoulder stress; ACE describes it as helping you stay steady with an upright trunk.

Slight forward lean (a few degrees from the hips) is common (Legion, others) and helps counter the pull; ACE warns that leaning too far forward, especially with too much weight, adds stress to the shoulder. FitPlate uses an upright or slightly forward-leaning torso (est. about 10–15 degrees at most) with the core braced.

Elbow bend: slight and fixed (about 15–30 degrees of bend, est., which is an elbow angle of about 150–165 degrees). Every source found that addresses it says to keep the elbows slightly bent throughout.
Chest up, shoulder blades gently back and down, ribs down, chin level, eyes forward.

Start (getting the handles): with the pulleys set, stand next to the stack, pick up the first handle with the near hand, then take the second handle with the other hand. Hold both with controlled tension and step into the staggered stance. Do not step far from the machine while holding the handles, and do not let a handle swing free.
Start, if the weight feels heavy: reduce the weight before you start; ask staff or a friend to hold one handle while you take the other. Never yank the handles to "wake up" the weight.

End (putting the handles back): with the arms in front and under control, let the arms open slowly until the weights are about to touch the stack lightly, then step back into the frame and release one handle at a time. Some sources step forward instead; both work, as long as the handle goes back slowly and does not snap back (Legion, Mighty, Fitwill). Never let go of a handle while the arms are fully open and tight.
If you cannot finish the last rep: do not let the arms fly open. Bring the hands together in front of your body, take a half step forward to slacken the cables, and lower the handles under control.

steps.title: Set the pulleys and pin
steps.action: Set both pulleys to the same height and put the pin in the same light plate on each stack.
steps.visualCheck: Front: both pulleys level; pins pushed in on both sides.

steps.title: Take the handles
steps.action: Take one handle in each hand, palms facing forward or down (overhand or neutral).
steps.feel: Light tension through the arms; grip firm but not tight.
steps.visualCheck: Front: both handles at the same height; wrists straight.

steps.title: Step into a staggered stance
steps.action: Take one stride forward with one foot, soften the front knee, and lean forward only a little.
steps.feel: Weight mostly on the front foot; core braced.
steps.visualCheck: Front: shoulders level; hips square. Side: slight lean, not hunched.

steps.title: Set the open position
steps.action: Open the arms out to the sides with the elbows slightly bent, until the hands are about in line with the shoulders; do not go behind the body line.
steps.feel: Gentle stretch across the chest and front shoulders.
steps.visualCheck: Front: elbows slightly bent and at about the same height as the shoulders or a little lower; hands in front of the shoulder line, not behind it.

steps.title: Start the arc
steps.action: Squeeze the chest and sweep both hands forward and inward as if hugging a large barrel; keep the elbow bend the same.
steps.feel: Chest working, not the arms bending.
steps.visualCheck: Front: both arms move together and at the same speed; elbows do not bend more.

steps.title: Bring the hands together
steps.action: Bring the handles together in front of the chest (or just cross them slightly), and squeeze for 1 second.
steps.feel: A firm squeeze in the middle of the chest.
steps.visualCheck: Front: handles meet at the midline at chest height; shoulders stay down, not shrugged.

steps.title: Open slowly
steps.action: Let the arms open along the same arc, slowly, until the hands are about in line with the shoulders.
steps.feel: Chest stretching under control; weights not crashing.
steps.visualCheck: Front: the weight stack moves smoothly; plates do not touch the rest of the stack.

steps.title: Repeat, then finish
steps.action: Repeat steps 5–7. After the last rep, bring the hands together in front, step back slightly into the frame, and put the handles down one at a time as in section 3, point 18.
steps.visualCheck: Both handles hang back at the pulleys; no handle swings.

commonMistakes.title: Too much weight
commonMistakes.text: Too much weight. Why: the elbows bend, the shoulders roll forward and the move turns into a poor press; ACE ties heavy loads and forward lean to shoulder stress. Fix: drop to a load you can control for 10–12 reps with 3–4 left.

commonMistakes.title: Bending and straightening the elbows during the rep
commonMistakes.text: Bending and straightening the elbows during the rep. Why: turns the fly into a press and loses the chest focus. Fix: freeze the elbow bend and "hug a barrel".

commonMistakes.title: Locking the elbows straight
commonMistakes.text: Locking the elbows straight. Why: puts load on the elbow joint and the biceps tendon. Fix: keep a soft bend.

commonMistakes.title: Letting the arms go far behind the body
commonMistakes.text: Letting the arms go far behind the body. Why: overstretches the front of the shoulder under load; one source advises keeping the elbows only slightly behind the back; no study of the exact mechanism was found. Fix: stop when the hands are about in line with the shoulders.

commonMistakes.title: Leaning far forward or swaying to swing the weight
commonMistakes.text: Leaning far forward or swaying to swing the weight. Why: more shoulder stress and less chest work. Fix: slight lean only; brace the core; lighter weight.

commonMistakes.title: Shrugging the shoulders up
commonMistakes.text: Shrugging the shoulders up. Why: the upper trapezius takes over and the neck tightens. Fix: shoulders down and away from the ears.

commonMistakes.title: Letting the stack slam or handles snap back
commonMistakes.text: Letting the stack slam or handles snap back. Why: jerky loading, noise, and risk of hitting yourself or a neighbour. Fix: lower under control; follow the end-of-set hand-off in section 3.

commonMistakes.title: Mismatched pulleys, pins or loads
commonMistakes.text: Mismatched pulleys, pins or loads. Why: one arm works harder and you twist. Fix: check both pulleys and pins before you start.

commonMistakes.title: Standing too far forward or too far back
commonMistakes.text: Standing too far forward or too far back. Why: a bad pull line and a shaky stance. Fix: one stride forward of the pulley line, staggered stance.

commonMistakes.title: Rushing the opening half
commonMistakes.text: Rushing the opening half. Why: the stretch phase is where control is lost. Fix: 3 seconds to open, 2 to close.

safetyNotes: Shoulder problems: the fly stretches the front of the shoulder under load; use a smaller range, a lighter load, a pec deck with the handles set forward, or a machine press, and ask a professional. ACE adds a tip on the standing incline fly: lower the resistance and keep the trunk upright.
High blood pressure: avoid breath-holding; breathe out as you close; moderate loads.
Lower back pain: use a braced staggered stance and an upright trunk; skip heavy leaning.
Pregnancy, recent surgery, osteoporosis, heart disease: see the table; ask a professional.

The 130/100 degree arm-to-shoulder-line thresholds, the 120–175 degree elbow band, the 10–15 degree lean limit, and the sets, reps and rest values are FitPlate choices (est.), not validated. A pulley-height EMG study, a clinical range-of-motion limit for the shoulder, a professional-body guide for handle release, and condition-specific sources for knee pain, lower back pain, obesity and PCOS are Not found.

conditionCautions.change: No breath-holding: breathe out as the hands close; light to moderate loads 10-15 reps, stop 3-4 reps before failure; no lifting if resting BP >= 180/120; uncontrolled BP: ask a doctor
conditionCautions.source: Valsalva systematic review 2013 (PubMed 23222073); NSCA 1999 article on Valsalva; Biology of Sport 2019 systematic review

conditionCautions.change: 2-3 non-consecutive resistance days per week; usual glucose checks if on insulin or sulfonylureas
conditionCautions.source: ADA position statement, Colberg et al. 2016

conditionCautions.change: After clearance: light load, 10-15 reps, continuous breathing, no straining
conditionCautions.source: AHA resistance exercise statement (via ACC summary 2023)

conditionCautions.change: Part of 2+ days per week resistance work with aerobic activity
Check you can stand comfortably in the frame; stable staggered stance; start light; machines may be easier if balance is hard; exercise-specific advice not found
